newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Lower Australia wheat crop seen still in safe.
newsitem.headline: Lower Australia wheat crop seen still in safe.

text.p: Australia would need to produce less than 11 million tonnes of wheat in the 1997/98 season for the current dry weather to have a big impact on international prices, a senior commodities analyst said on Friday.

Brendan Hillary, client adviser at ANZ Futures Ltd, told an agricultural commodities conference this happened during the 1994 (April/March) season, but he said fundamentals were considerably different in that year. This year it appeared that the rest of the world had a reasonable crop, with only Australia and Argentina "doing it tough," Hillary said.
Provided Australia grew more than 11 million tonnes, it would receive world prices for its wheat, Hillary said.
Selling wheat futures in Sydney and buying futures in Chicago would seem to provide a reasonable opportunity, he said.

The conference was presented with a mixed picture of Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop prospects, although speakers did not suggest that production was likely to fall below Hillary's 11 million tonne figure.

The El Nino weather pattern appeared to be affecting only a small part of Australia, with good opening rains in most of Western Australia, Queensland and much of New South Wales, said Brendan Stewart, president of Grains Council of Australia.
Rains in the February-April period had resulted in very favourable moisture reserves in these states, he said.
"Nevertheless, the timing of further rainfall over the rest of winter will determine the final size of the crop," he said.

The potential for poorer than normal growing conditions had prompted the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) to forecast a 1997/98 wheat crop of 16.3 million tonnes, down just over 30 percent from last year's record production of 23.5 million, he noted.
ABARE was also forecasting an export value for the 1997/98 wheat crop of A$2.5 billion, down 40 percent from last year's record of almost A$4.2 billion.
ABARE has forecast a 1997/98 coarse grains crop of 7.6 million tonnes, down 26 percent from last year's production of 10.3 million tonnes.
ABARE's forecast export value for the 1997/98 coarse grains crop of A$586 million is down by 48.6 percent from last year's export value of just over A$1.1 billion.
"However, it is still too early to tell what the final outcome of this year's harvest will be due to uncertainty over weather conditions," Stewart said.
The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) was optimistic that export availability from major exporters was likely to be down by five to seven million tonnes, he said.
Australian wheat shipments for 1996/97 have totalled 16.4 million tonnes so far.

Furthermore, despite the liklihood of China's imports remaining at relatively low levels, the AWB considered that import demand was likely to remain relatively strong largely due to increases in import requirements by Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey and India, Stewart said.
Imports for these five countries doubled in 1996/97 to 14 million tonnes from seven million tonnes, he said.

The AWB believed that the same five markets would have an even stronger import requirement in 1997/98, with imports likely to increase a further 4.0-4.5 million tonnes to 18.0-18.5 million tonnes, Stewart said.
"Overall, the AWB beleives it is likely that world demand will outstrip supply, resulting in a drawdown of stocks."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
